The US Director of National Intelligence, Jay Clayton, said an investigation is under way into Alice Huang and her company, Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre firm. «There is an ongoing investigation into her company and her,» he said. On Sunday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent stated in a television interview that the administration wants answers from Nvidia regarding chip sales to China: who was monitoring compliance with the rules and which levels of the company knew.

The affair is weighing on the markets. On Friday, Nvidia stock lost around 13% following news that the SEC, the US stock market regulator, is examining the company's accounting, according to two sources cited by the press. The slump in artificial intelligence-related stocks swept across Wall Street and Asian stock markets, where among the causes cited by analysts is precisely the scandal involving Nvidia, which has reopened calls for tighter restrictions on China's access to advanced chips.

According to the Departments of Commerce and Justice, the investigation into Megaspeed began in 2024 over possible export control violations. Alice Huang was questioned during an on-site inspection in June 2025; the criminal case was subsequently referred to the Department of Justice. An associate of Huang, Li Ming, is out on bail in Singapore: the city-state's charges relate to alleged false declarations to Super Micro Computer and do not name Megaspeed. Singapore police said they found insufficient evidence of offences linked to inaccurate statements by Huang, who received a stern warning for providing information believed to be knowingly inaccurate and for downplaying her role. Singapore has not investigated her for espionage.

According to a US press report, Alice Huang was allegedly in contact with an official from a major Chinese intelligence agency from spring 2025 to autumn 2026; there is no official confirmation. According to another account, the Department of Justice is verifying whether companies linked to Huang helped ship Super Micro products out of the US to China. German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil said that the bank must explain «with absolute transparency» how it has remedied the deficiencies.

The lead azide had been stored for decades and, according to the government, had deteriorated to the point where it could explode on its own, especially with falling temperatures. One figure does not match the other: the weight indicated by sources fluctuates between approximately 4.5 and 5 tonnes.

Fifteen minutes after the explosion, four stations of the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) did not detect lead in the air, and the readings remained unchanged two hours later. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) also reported that it had not found lead. Adam Telle, the acting Secretary of the Army, said that the weather was ideal. The outgoing Governor of Iowa, Kim Reynolds, spoke of a positive outcome, and the Governor of Missouri, Mike Kehoe, said that the explosion remained well contained.

President Donald Trump wrote on social media that the protective measures exceeded expectations. The president of COP31 in Antalya, Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, wants to bring the third draft of the final decision to the plenary without further changes. According to European delegation sources, the European Union intends to vote against, and under the consensus rule this is enough to prevent approval. Kurum says there is a broad consensus, with a few minor open issues, and that those blocking the process should reflect on their position.

The draft, presented overnight between Saturday and Sunday, does not explicitly mention the phase-out of fossil fuels, but recalls «in its entirety» the UAE Consensus, the final document of COP28 in Dubai in 2023. That text provided for the transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems by 2050. Kurum says he is convinced the text is acceptable to all parties.

Negotiations, involving almost 200 delegations, were scheduled to end on Friday 20 November and have continued for a second day past the deadline. Delegations could submit objections until 3 am Greenwich Mean Time on Sunday, and the session to begin approval was set for 6 am, 7 am in Italy. Decisions are taken by consensus: an objection from a single country can block them.

The French Minister for Ecological Transition, Monique Barbut, called the proposal a step backwards and said «time is running out and we are not there yet». Thursday's draft had removed all references to fossil fuels following objections from Saudi Arabia and other major oil and gas producers, drawing strong criticism. One hundred civil society organisations wrote to Turkey and Australia, who are leading the negotiations, warning that the summit risks being «one of the most disappointing COPs» ever organized by the UN. The European Union is calling for an explicit commitment to phase out fossil fuels; the Arab group of countries and Russia refuse to include it.

The third draft, in Article 38, calls for the «full and rapid» implementation of nationally determined contributions, namely each country's climate commitments, and of national adaptation plans. Kurum states that the text also addresses the concerns of developing countries regarding adaptation funding. According to reports, discussions remain open on how much effort to ask from countries to reduce coal, oil and gas, whether to encourage carbon capture and storage, and whether the expansion of electricity should be based solely on renewables or also on gas and coal.

This is the first COP since the UN confirmed that global warming will exceed the 1.5-degree limit of the Paris Agreement.

On Saturday 21 November, the Russian cargo ship Sparta II caught fire in the Gulf of Finland after being hit by two drones. The 16 crew members were evacuated on lifeboats and transferred to another vessel. Russia says the attack took place about three nautical miles from its border; according to the Finnish Ministry of Defence, it occurred in international waters, west of the island of Gogland.

The 121-metre-long ship is operated by Oboronlogistika, a company linked to the Russian Ministry of Defence, and is under US and Ukrainian sanctions for transporting military material. It had departed on Friday from Saint Petersburg and was bound for Kaliningrad, the Russian exclave on the Baltic. Having been hit, it lost steering capability and drifted into Finnish territorial waters, near Loviisa, where it is now anchored.

The spokesman for the Finnish armed forces, Aki-Mauri Huhtinen, says Ukraine's responsibility is likely, without explaining the motive for the attack. Ilja Iljin, of the Border Guard, warns that explosions are possible and that the ship could sink if the fire continues; extinguishing it could take days or weeks. The cargo has not been identified and the Border Guard does not rule out that it includes military material. So far, no environmental damage has been detected.

Ukraine has not claimed responsibility for the action. Vladyslav Vlasiuk, sanctions advisor to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote that ships sanctioned by Kyiv have «a rather unfortunate tendency to catch fire» and that he does not think this is the last incident. The governor of the Leningrad region, Aleksandr Drozdenko, states that overnight Russian air defence shot down 80 drones over the region, and the governor of Kaliningrad says the incident does not threaten supplies to the exclave.

On Saturday, during the rescue operations, a suspected Russian helicopter briefly entered Finnish airspace, up to 4.1 kilometres beyond the border, near Loviisa. Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen suggests a link to the rescue operations; the Border Guard is investigating. The Finnish Prime Minister, Petteri Orpo, said the war is spreading to neighbouring countries. Helsinki has introduced temporary restrictions on air and sea traffic in the eastern part of the gulf. A Russian tugboat, intervening at Finland's request, has been tasked with towing the vessel towards the area of Russian responsibility. Estonia and Sweden took part in the operations.

The UN climate summit, COP31, closed on Sunday 22 November in Antalya, Turkey, without a final agreement, after a prolonged extension. The text presented by the co-presidencies of Turkey and Australia was rejected by the European Union and other countries because it made no mention of fossil fuels. According to sources' reconstructions, it is the first failure of an annual climate conference since the Copenhagen summit in 2009.

The draft would have recognised for the first time in an official text that global warming is on a trajectory exceeding 1.5 degrees. In the revised version, the target of 120 billion dollars to help poor countries adapt had been removed. Delegates from various countries described the text as too weak to address warming.

The European Union said it would not approve an agreement «that does not even mention fossil fuels». Denmark's Climate Minister, Samira Nawa, explained that the EU would have accepted the clauses on adaptation funds, but that strong commitments on emission reductions and reference to science were lacking. For British negotiator Kate Hughes, the draft «takes us backwards from the science».

The front opposed to the word «fossils» includes oil- and gas-producing countries. The Saudi Arabian delegation said that «climate change requires all solutions on the table» and that «concrete solutions» must not be taken away. The Russian delegate, Sergei Kononuchenko, said Russia «cannot accept any wording on fossil fuels», warning that less oil and gas supply could lead to energy poverty. Iraq expressed «deep concern» over passages it said move away from the Paris Agreement.

Island and most vulnerable nations spoke of betrayal. The Marshall Islands say they were «disappointed by all sides», Vanuatu called the silence on fossils unacceptable, and the group of least developed countries, 44 nations with over a billion inhabitants, said it could not accept steps backwards. Kenya complained that the text did not respond to Africa's needs.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres said he was «deeply disappointed». Chris Bowen, Australia's Climate Minister and chair of the negotiations, said that «an obvious issue is the transition away from fossil fuels» and that some parties would veto any text mentioning it. Murat Kurum, the Turkish Environment Minister and president of COP31, said there will be no new text and that work will focus on implementing decisions already taken.

From January, the price cap on gas and electricity in Great Britain will rise by 26%. This was announced on Wednesday by Ofgem, the British energy regulator, and the annual bills of millions of households will exceed £2,000.

It is the third consecutive increase in the cap, quarter after quarter. According to reports, this is the first time since the gas crisis following the Russian invasion of Ukraine that the annual bill has exceeded that threshold.

The increase stems from the rise in wholesale gas prices, which had not been seen since the first winter after the invasion. The cap applies to standard tariffs: those with a fixed-price contract are not affected by the rise.

The government has already announced a £100 payment, which millions of households will receive from January. The available sources do not indicate which households are eligible or how the increase will be offset.

According to measurements by the National Weather Service, about 39 centimetres accumulated in Hollywood in 72 hours. The mayor of Hollywood, Josh Levy, asked residents to document the damage in order to access potential state and federal aid. The Brightline train between Orlando and West Palm Beach was suspended on Friday and resumed on Saturday.
